speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: More workers today are also caregivers and women, who traditionally take up caregiving roles, continue to face the balancing act between work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At the same time, our enterprises are navigating an uncertain global environment marked by higher costs and rising trade barriers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Alongside these changes, more Singaporeans are choosing platform work as a livelihood of choice, whether for flexibility, autonomy or income stability.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And layered onto all of these is the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), which is already beginning to transform the very nature of work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Not just the jobs we do, but how work is organised, how skills are built and how careers evolve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Against this backdrop, Singapore's manpower policies must not only balance global talent attraction with local workforce protection, but must actively enable Singaporeans to thrive as workplaces evolve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In the last term of Government, MOM and our tripartite partners worked together to guide our workforce out of the COVID-19 crisis and enabled workers to benefit from the recovery.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We secured better terms for lower-wage workers as well as platform workers, improved caregivers' access to flexible work arrangements (FWAs) and took early steps to prepare for a super-aged society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But as this new term begins, our labour and industry transformation policies face a far more complex task.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It can augment workers or displace them, depending on how work and jobs are redesigned.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The key question is not whether transformation will happen.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is whether it will translate into stronger wages, deeper skills and better career pathways for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But AI is reshaping industries at a speed that demands sharper, more dynamic responses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: While some ITMs have been refreshed and augmented with Job Transformation Maps, we must now ensure they provide clear direction on: AI-driven business process redesign, timelines for workforce transition and credible pathways into new roles when existing ones are sunsetted.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Equally important, we must ensure that employers bring their workforce along this journey.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As industries transform, workplaces must become more inclusive and supportive, particularly for mid-career workers and those with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Recent platform exits remind us that workers remain vulnerable to sudden business decisions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At the same time, road safety is an increasing concern.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As more Singaporeans rely on platform work as a primary livelihood, we must guard against platform consolidation creating a race to the bottom in payouts and incentives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When platform exit, workers should not be left exposed to delayed or unpaid dues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Stronger safeguards are needed to ensure timely notice fulfilment of payment obligations and clear records, whether defaults occur while also strengthening protections for their safety on the roads.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The Platform Workers Trilateral Group demonstrated in 2025 how effective collaboration can address complex challenges, such as illegal platform work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Going forward, platform worker associations should and must remain a central pillar, strengthening partnerships to improve both livelihood resilience and safety outcomes for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Today, my Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) colleagues and fellow labour Members of Parliament (MPs) will share our views on how manpower policies must continue to secure good jobs for our Singaporean core, while powering economic progress within this land and infrastructural constraints of our little red dot.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Because of this remains a delicate but necessary balancing act.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must enable time-crunched mid-career workers to upskill; without placing unsustainable pressure on employers in a tight labour market.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must provide assurance to IHL students entering a workforce where entry-level roles are evolving.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must ensure local-foreign workforce complementarity remains responsive, without compromising business agility.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And we must strengthen income security, as workforce churn rises, skills half-lives shorten, caregiving burdens grow and cost pressures persist.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: There are limits to how much we can expand our foreign workforce, given infrastructure constraints and our social capacity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Our manpower strategy must therefore focus on transformation, not substitution.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Firms must become less manpower-reliant even as they become more productive.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: And our local workforce must move up the skills ladder alongside industry transformations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In this new phase of labour transformation, I would like to put forward three Budget priorities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: First, we must continue attracting top global talent in a way that strengthens, not substitutes our Singaporean core.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This requires stronger complementarity frameworks, clearer skills transfer expectations and leadership pathways for our locals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Second, as businesses face tighter margins, we must support transformation, not dependency on manpower expansion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Mr Chairman, our approach to foreign manpower must go beyond access.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The NTS-OL is an important tool to address manpower shortages in critical roles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: But as we expand it, we must ensure that access to foreign manpower does not simply relieve short-term labour gaps.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: It must actively support upgrading and reframing of jobs are they transform with AI and technology into attractive jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I therefore call on the Ministry to accompany this expansion with clear productivity-linked conditions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Firms that access NTS-OL manpower should also commit to structured training for locals, skills transfer from foreign workers and job redesign that improves work processes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Where appropriate, access to NTS-OL manpower should be tied to demonstrable workforce upgrading plans, including career pathways for Singaporeans and measurable productivity improvements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Second, we should ensure that expansion does not suppress wage growth for vulnerable local workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The Budget should support firms in redesigning jobs alongside workforce diversification so that productivity gains translate into higher wages, not simply labour cost substitutions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This means embedding progression pathways, leadership pipelines and skills upgrading for locals into sectors where NTS-OL access is expanded.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Foreign manpower must complement transformation, not replace it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: If done right, this expansion can raise productivity across the workforce and support sustainable growth that delivers better wages and good jobs for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Employment Act was last reviewed in 2018.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That review coincided with the act's 50th anniversary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It follows that the broadening of coverage makes the current review of the Employment Act more significant than previous iterations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was first announced at the Committee of Supply (COS) last year when MOM announced its plans to review the act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost immediately, the Singapore National Employers Federation moved quickly to caveat that the review should not, and I quote, "inadvertently mandate progressive employment practices that may reduce flexibilities for employers and undermine business competitiveness".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There have been little further announcements on the areas under review beyond the broad objectives which were announced when the Tripartite Workgroup first met in August last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There has been some speculation of specific enhancements, including raising the minimum statutory annual leave entitlement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Any increase through proposed amendments to the act here would be akin to pushing against an open door if proposed amendments substantively amount to what is a common market practice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share what deliberations have taken place thus far, and if there has been a significant gap in positions between the Ministry, the unions and employer organisations like the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF)?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What areas of amendment have been scuttled or deferred to date in view of divergences in position?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Will the Ministry consider a public consultation in parallel with tripartite negotiations, given the significantly larger number of workers covered by the Employment Act today?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, the Government should review its tripartite posture to lean on the side of workers more, particularly in today's employment landscape.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Prime Minister observed in this year's Budget speech, we must always take care of our own.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One long-standing anomaly in the Act is the distinction between workmen and non-workmen, a distinction that has arguably blurred in today's environment of AI skills upgrading and job convergence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are there plans to achieve parity with regard to salary thresholds for workmen and non-workmen alike?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, both the Act and the tripartite guidelines envisage the payment of retrenchment benefits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Previous MOM surveys indicate that in general, a very large number of companies, around 90%, are already able to pay retrenchment benefits to the level of the tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The time has come for these guidelines to be legislated as a norm in an advanced economy like Singapore, as a manifestation of a basic Singapore standard for all workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on MOM's own data on retrenchments, legislating for a reasonable quantum of retrenchment benefits that are already the overwhelming norm in Singapore would not be an earth-shattering legislative development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, doing so would be consistent with the objective of commitments like #Every Worker Matters and a "we first" society.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you may take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am aware that the review is ongoing and I declare my interest as part of the tripartite workgroup on the review.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am therefore asking for MOM now to provide an update to the House on when they plan to roll out the amendments and in what broad areas, pursuant to some of my lobbying efforts in this House the past few years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To avoid conflicts of interest and undermining management effectiveness, executives with senior management functions were excluded from collective bargaining.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can I request MOM to look into providing greater clarity through a firmer and clearer articulation on this point, either through amending the guidelines or amending the Industrial Relations Act for statutory clarity?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: More than two years ago, MOM announced that these guidelines were being developed in consultation with tripartite partners, with the intention to provide clearer guidance to employers and better protection for employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At that point, we were told that the guidelines were expected to be released by the end of 2024.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yet, many employees, especially professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), continue to face broad and restrictive restraint of trade clauses that can limit their mobility, bargaining power and career progression, even where there is no legitimate business interest to protect.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Could the Minister update this House on the current status of this and indicate when employers and workers can expect clear and practical guidance to be issued?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And in the interim, what advice does MOM have for employees who may be subject to overly restrictive or unreasonable restraint of trade clauses today?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the decades, in my work with the Labour Movement, I have worked alongside thousands of workers who lost their jobs, sometimes with notice, sometimes overnight, often with little clarity on what comes next.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is a human event, affecting livelihoods, families and dignity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since the start of the scheme, can MOM provide an update on the scheme?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, notification often comes after retrenchment decisions have been finalised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Early notification enables early intervention and early intervention saves jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to suggest that the Ministry consider extending free or subsidised access to AI premium tools to a larger group of Singaporeans, such as all mature workers, on a time-limited basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these premium tools cost no more than US$20 a month, or under $30 a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Six months of fully or partly subsidised access, could make a significant difference in helping people become familiar with and experiment with AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, the fear of missing out could prompt people to try the tools for the first time, which they may put off despite the availability of free versions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these tools are intuitive and can be adopted even without special training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Given the potential for an AI divide where the affluent and less well-off have differential access to premium AI tools, a further suggestion is to offer lower-income Singaporeans subsidised access to premium AI tools on a longer-term basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This would help ensure that AI adoption remains inclusive and does not widen existing inequalities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One of my closest friends, whom I have known since I was 13, is a banker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This in and of itself is unremarkable, since the financial sector accounts for one in every 16 workers in our labour force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is remarkable, however, is how he got there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My mate, trained in architecture, obtaining his bachelor's and master's degrees in the subject, but after graduation, he applied for and scored his first job in investment banking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Why did the bank bother interviewing him to begin with?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: According to him, they were impressed by his sharpness and moxie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There was a reason that they would teach him everything that he would need to know on the job anyhow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, he an immensely successful financier leading the Asia Pacific business of a top-shelf asset management firm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The story illustrates a reality that all of us are familiar with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In spite of the best efforts of educators, like myself, most of the skills needed for our jobs are not learnt in the classroom but in life settings on-the-job training (OJT).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, OJT, which could involve formally organised structures, such as apprenticeships or internships, or more informal processes, such as guidance and mentorship, often imparts specialised skills that are typically far more valuable for the actual day-to-day performance of one's job than the validation conferred by a certification itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But by emphasising paper qualifications, the assessment only pathway continues to be hamstrung by an insistence on assessment over demonstration, on the acquisition of certification over experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those I have spoken to shared that it has become more of an impediment rather than a genuine stepping stone toward career advancement in the skills trades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Workforce Singapore (WSG) runs existing Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs), but these are mostly linked to industry transformation maps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In practice, the industries covered are linked, limited to professional and technical roles rather than broad based.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: WSG also runs a career trial for employers where firms can try the employee out for some time with Government support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This helps spread the risk for employers in terms of hiring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is less clear how trainees, especially those who are seeking to retrain and reskill, gain structured systematic exposure to new skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a major step and one that I wholeheartedly support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But a quick search reveals less than 100 open positions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, in his National Day Rally, announcing the initiative, spoke about scaling up the programme if the economy worsens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the economy is doing well, I believe that GRIT's time has come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Agentic AI threatens to replace the need for entry-level positions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, without a pipeline to train new hires, especially on the job, it will be a conundrum, a shortage of experienced mid-level workers which remain in high demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presently, securing GRIT positions is largely decentralised, relying primarily on proactive posting by the hiring entity or a small number of private jobs clearing houses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Polytechnics and some university programmes do sponsor internships, but only for students that have first completed their coursework components.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most programmes accepting apprenticeships focus on technical or professional disciplines, such as finance, technology, medicine or law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These facts mean that the benefits of OJT will tend to accrue to only limited segments of the labour force and indeed, the majority of current listings are for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) or finance graduates, many of whom already possess the means to seek, identify and apply to such opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is substantive evidence that internships and apprenticeships do not only contribute to enhance knowledge transfer and more efficient production but can also play a role in reducing the extent of labour market polarisation, which is becoming a growing concern in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, such systems tend to be more successful when operating within the rubric of a larger institutional framework.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A national level institution would establish the standard rules behind each party's commitments, promote worker firm matching and encourage the movement of journeymen to other firms once they have completed their formal training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, by taking the lead in establishing a nationally recognised internship and apprenticeship programme that enables voluntary progressive acquisition of certifications, the Government can also codify a learning culture that opens up the substantial benefits of such experiences to a much wider range of candidates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Non-academic pursuits, such as the culinary arts, music and sports; artisanal practices, such as horology, furniture making and other skilled crafts; and professions that rely on experience and OJT rather than book smarts alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This national OJT system can be strengthened by two further elements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, uplifting the wages and work prospects of our lower-wage workers is fundamental to building a truly "we first" society, one where progress is shared and no worker is left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Progressive Wage Model (PWM) has delivered significant gains over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This reversal, though modest, is a warning signal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we are serious about inclusive growth, the wage growth for lower-wage workers must consistently outpace that of the median, not merely keep pace with it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The increase in the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) is welcome.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Employers must drive business and workforce transformation so that productivity gains are built into lower-wage roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The strength of PWM lies in linking wages to skills, responsibilities and productivity, rather than imposing a blunt wage floor.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If not, what further interventions will be introduced?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Workers must be supported to upskill and reskill to strengthen career mobility, especially as AI reshapes our economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Access to training must become smarter and more targeted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge MOM to leverage AI to personalise SkillsFuture course recommendations, integrated into National Trade Union Congress' (NTUC's) AI-enabled career coach, so that workers receive clear guidance on their next skills pathway.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The question is not whether jobs will change, but whether lower-wage workers will benefit from the change rather than be displaced by it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call on the Government to work very closely with tripartite partners to co-develop AI-augmented roles and to update skills frameworks, so that technology adoption translates into measurable productivity gains, better job quality and stronger wage progression particularly in PWM sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, the question before us is simple.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As Singapore advances, will our lower-wage workers advance faster?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us recommit to ensuring that the ladder of progress remains firmly within reach and that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It was set at $24,000 in 2012 before being consistently raised every few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In contrast, the income thresholds for the Workfare Income Supplement have gone from $1,700 pre-2013 to $1,900 in 2013, to $2,500 in 2023, to $3,000 in 2025.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While this may seem comparable, the truth is that the most recent bout of inflation hits the poorest the most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is because the categories where prices rose the most, notably food, transport and rent, consume a disproportionate share of the incomes of those in the lower end of the distribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is a conclusion backed by ample research, both in Singapore and the rest of the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is true that this may be partially offset by nominal wage gains that bolster purchasing power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it is unclear if this is the case.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: NTUC has embarked on a study with the Singapore University of Technology and Design, and will share more soon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We realise this is often fuelled by mismatch in jobs, skills and expectations of employers, including job seekers both young and not so young.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There may be occasions where underemployment may occur as a result of this mismatch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: We should monitor this closely and provide proper career counselling, coaching and mentoring at all stages of a person's career from his/her first job, during his/her first job, when looking for the next job or beyond retirement and re-employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the same vein, I suggest both individual and employer SkillsFuture credits be approved for use towards professional career coaching, guidance, mentoring and counselling services for workers and individuals beyond those currently provided by our IHLs, WSG and e2i.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As AI automates many entry level tasks, firms are increasingly prioritising candidates who are immediately productive over fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Without access to quality roles soon after graduation, many of our youths risk a long-term scarring effect, where early joblessness correlates to lower lifetime earnings, skills atrophy and even social and civic alienation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Before I continue, I wish to declare that I am a director and shareholder of a company which is a small and medium enterprise (SME).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This ensures that graduates gain access to quality roles and structured training while the Government offsets the initial costs of onboarding.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Targeting these wage credits in micro and small enterprises empowers these smaller businesses to offer more competitive wages, helping them to compete for talent against medium and larger enterprises.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To address employers' concern of young recruits leaving soon after being trained, the Government could fund an additional 20% of a one-month retention bonus to be paid out only on the first anniversary of employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I propose that this scheme be implemented for an initial three years period with a robust assessment of its effectiveness before any extension.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, while GRIT offers temporary three- to six-month placements, it does not guarantee the stability of full-time employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This proposal encourages permanent hiring from day one.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Youth Wage Credit Scheme shifts the focus from temporary trainingships to immediate stable SME employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By incentivising permanent hires, it buffers against AI-driven displacement and ensures Singapore's next generation enters the workforce with greater security and confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: With our ageing population, jobs in nursing and healthcare will continue to grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: While generative AI (GenAI) may pose risks to various white collar occupations, jobs which require manual skills or dexterity remain comparatively resilient to automation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Skilled trades like technicians and mechanics are not so easily automated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: However, many young Singaporeans do not aspire to careers in healthcare and skilled trades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: This will increase our reliance on foreign manpower for essential roles, while making it hard to fulfil the job aspirations of our young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: The reality is that not all Singaporeans can be professionals or corporate executives in a highly competitive and technologically driven global economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Many will have to build careers in services and skilled trades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Wages are an important consideration and the pay in these jobs must rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Yet job attractiveness also depends on whether work is meaningful and how it is perceived by society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: My question is whether we can be bolder in redesigning jobs, such as nursing, security and skilled trades, at scale so that they become occupations our young people aspire to pursue, so that AI and robotics take over the tedious aspects of work, while workers contribute to service design, innovation and customer engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: There should be more jobs, like Advanced Practice Nurses, offering greater professional responsibility with commensurate remuneration and recognition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: The aim should be to develop roles that integrate head, heart and hand competencies, making them more resilient to AI and automation as well as more appealing to Singaporeans than single-dimensional jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: There is a second aspect of job redesign I would like to highlight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: As organisations review work processes to harness AI and automation, we need stronger capabilities for human-centric job redesign, ensuring that AI augments rather than replaces human contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: I remain optimistic about the unique value that people bring notwithstanding the rapid development of more powerful AI models.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: This is because AI models lack consciousness, they do not have an innate sense of right and wrong, and they are trained based on past or existing data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Recognising these limits can help us identify the uniquely human strengths that should shape job redesign.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: I hope that Singapore can show the way in human-centric job redesign and would like to ask whether the Ministry has plans to develop deeper expertise in this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: Last year, while attending a conference in Astana, I joined a day tour led by a young guide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: He brought me on a short hike to a hilltop overlooking a lake, which was not a typical tourist destination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: It was where his grandparents had brought him as a child to play.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: That personal story and human connection to a place, created an experience that no electronic guide or AI could replicate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho
text: This gives me hope that even in an AI-enabled future, human insight, empathy and storytelling will remain central to meaningful work.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a good sign of uptake, but uptake does not tell us if there has been a meaningful shift in how employers evaluate and hire candidates.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tools can change how workers present their skills, but tools alone cannot change hiring behaviour.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If employers continue to hire based on degrees and past job titles, then the passport risks becoming, as my colleague Andre described yesterday, a digital filing cabinet.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Singapore made meaningful progress in adopting skills-first practices, key gaps, such as business adoption of skills first hiring and stronger ecosystem coordination, remained.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a capability gap, not a values problem.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new Statutory Board formed by the merger of WSG and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) was announced as a one-stop shop for workers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, for the new agency to develop practical tool kits that employers can use for portfolio-based assessment and skills-first hiring.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: How effective it has been since its start especially now with the doing away of the Fair Consideration Framework triple-weak watchlist?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some recruiters have candidly shared with me that they only post on MyCareersFuture portal if they must fulfil the Government's requirements to put up the job for 14 days before they can hire foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: If that is the case, it will be hard for the Government to have a good sensing of all the available job openings in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Would MOM consider mobilising and/or requiring all companies to post their available openings on the portal for ease of tracking, analytics and sensemaking of industry hiring needs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: By the same token, there are those whom I have heard comply with the 14-day posting requirement merely as window dressing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Likewise, a closer scrutiny of employment agencies is much needed at this juncture as sometimes such breaches and window dressing are carried out by them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I urge MOM to pay a close watch on this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On the second point on human capital practitioners, especially their practices and processes are really key to foster a fair and inclusive workplace including one with a strong Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am aware that the IHRP is doing good work to certify human capital practitioners with the IHRP certification.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I declare my interest as co-chair of the workgroup looking at human capital development.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Can MOM progressively then mandate the certification of HR practitioners, now that we have this IHRP certification in place?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the interim, perhaps companies should consider having at least one IHRP-certified HR professional before they can be allowed to hire any foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In the same vein, I suggest that employers be allowed to use their Enterprise SkillsFuture credits, similar to what workers have, for sending their HR staff for IHRP training and certification.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, businesses support the principle of a strong Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Foreign manpower must remain complementary, not a substitute.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That social compact is fundamental and must be upheld.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, what we are seeing is not a marginal adjustment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is a structural reset of labour cost baselines.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But taken together, they represent a meaningful shift in cost structure, particularly for sectors where the local manpower pool remains limited despite best efforts.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the higher end, Singapore competes to anchor regional headquarters and specialised mandates.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Location decisions are increasingly marginal between Singapore and other hubs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When higher EP thresholds are layered onto elevated rentals, energy and compliance costs, the cumulative effect matters.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Missed mandates and unanchored teams can quietly narrow future job creation for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the S Pass, the pressure is even more immediate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Domestic-oriented sectors, such as food and beverages (F&B), retail and other labour-intensive sectors, operate on thin margins.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Further cost escalation leaves two paths: raise prices, contributing to cost-of-living pressures; or compress operations, reducing service levels and employment scale.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, these same sectors are supporting wage uplifts for lower-wage Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If viability weakens, the very workers we seek to uplift may face slower hiring and progression.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On LQS, let me be clear: uplifting lower-wage Singaporeans is a national priority, and employers support this direction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is not principle, but pace and calibration, especially when multiple levers move concurrently.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Firms are encouraged to upgrade foreign manpower quality.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, levy increases across skill tiers mean that both upgrading and retention are becoming more expensive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When cost differentials narrow, the incentive to upgrade may weaken.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The question, therefore, is how we preserve three objectives simultaneously: safeguarding the social compact, preserving Singapore's competitiveness and sustaining long-term employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a structured framework to assess sectoral sensitivity, particularly in industries with thin margins or limited automation pathways?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And are there mechanisms to recalibrate if unintended economic effects begin to emerge?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If we calibrate carefully, Singapore can remain both competitive and cohesive, a place where businesses grow, investments anchor and Singaporeans thrive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare that I am the group managing director of Commonwealth Capital Group, a Singapore global enterprise that stewards more than 1,000 livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: A core part of the Government's agenda is jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition to an income, jobs provide dignity, meaning and confidence to our workers – something that Government handouts cannot fulfil.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I would add that the Government should embrace the philosophy that to be pro-worker, our policies also have to be pro-business.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We should see companies as platforms and partners for the Government to achieve its policy goals.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: One, we want to keep seniors employed longer and ideally on similar salary terms as when they were younger, even if their productivity declines.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, we want to narrow income inequality by uplifting wages at the lower end, even above productivity levels of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, we want jobseekers to find jobs as soon as possible, even if it means they have to acquire skills on the job in order to do the job well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: From the perspective of employers, hiring is seldom short-term.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies plan more than one year in advance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore suggest that MOM's policies incorporate two more principles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, as Mr Mark Lee also said, companies should be given more time to adjust and adapt to policy changes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, companies should be given more longer-term direction instead of annual, effectively ad hoc grant extensions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Why not just commit to a longer-term extension, with employers given two years' notice of any change?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, the PWCS can be made more longer term.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Or why not fold this into the permanent Workfare scheme?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This is particularly important if technology changes widen productivity gaps beyond what is reasonable for our lower wage workers to close despite all their effort.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government already has a working model today in the form of Career Conversion Programmes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In my proposal, we should then not need to impose a different job or different sector requirement for those who are looking for a job for more than six months.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This effectively covers Mr Gerald Giam's proposal for our youths who are looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: This will definitely do a good job in alleviating the job-related anxieties that many of our Members have raised.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, technology does not transform companies, people do.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want sustained growth, enterprises and workers must transform together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not AI first and people later, it is together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why the implementation of the enterprise workforce transformation package matters.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many firms are investing in AI and automation, and that is good.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But the real test is this: are we redesigning jobs or just reducing headcount?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must make job redesign a default expectation of enterprise transformation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When a logistics SME adopted AI route optimisation, they did not cut drivers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They trained them in digital fleet coordination and customer management.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In precision engineering, AI-enabled inspection reduced manual checks.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead of displacement, technicians were reskilled into robotics maintenance and data functions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the model we want: adopt technology, redesign jobs, reskill workers and reshare the gains.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: SMEs face real constraints: cost, capability and confusion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If assessing support requires navigating multiple schemes and agencies, we will lose them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Who supports my training and how will my wages progress?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mid-career and low-wage workers in particular must see tangible progression not just of digitalisation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, will MOM publish outcome indicators, such as the number of jobs redesigned and wage progression outcomes?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, how will advisory support for SMEs be strengthened to ensure AI adoption leads to job upgrading, not displacement?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And fourth, how will MOM support gig workers and self-employed persons whose rice bowls are broken by AI?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, enterprise transformation is necessary, but workforce transformation is non-negotiable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Growth must upgrade our workers, or it will not last.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The median age of workers is now 45, and as industries transform, many mid-career PMEs face heightened risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Like preventive health checks, this diagnostic would assess skills readiness and digital gaps, role fit and mobility options; and transition risks, especially in sectors seeing softening demand, such as professional services, manufacturing and information and communications technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Higher risk cases will receive a short human coaching review directly linked to MyCareersFuture for follow-through.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A standardised screening, paired with human support, helps PMEs take early action and helps employers anticipate redeployment and workforce transformation needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But employers, especially SMEs, need stronger support to redesign roles, retrain staff and hire mid-career candidates.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mid-career renewal will affect nearly every PME's working life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will expand on strengthening human resources (HR) capabilities in my other COS cut later.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population and longer lifespans, drawing on evidence-based frameworks, including the Stanford longevity model, we can mainstream a national career taxonomy across the build, consolidate, retrain and transition stages.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This provides a shared language for both workers and employers, enabling better planning, clearer expectations and more proactive career decisions at each career's life stage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, supporting the career health and employability of our mature PMEs require a new national compact built on shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Government must provide early signal tools, accessible support and clear pathways.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Employers must redesign work and invest in mid-career renewal.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Workers must take ownership of their lifelong career health.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we get this right, PMEs will have the clarity, confidence and capabilities to stay employable and contribute meaningfully across longer, more fulfilling careers, ensuring Singapore's workforce stays resilient as we age.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I rise to speak on creating diverse pathways to success through skilled trades and the mindset shift we need as a society to recognise hands-on work as essential, skilled and worthy of respect.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: During these debates, much has been said about the rise of AI and its multiple uses.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: However, let us not forget that every day, Singapore runs on the work of people who fix our lifts, maintain our estates, keep the kitchen running, service our vehicles, install electrical systems and respond when things break down.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They are jobs that require craft, discipline, judgement and often years to hone.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want a strong local labour core, we have to value these jobs, these roles, not just in words, but in how we treat these workers and how we design progression for them.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is an important signal, because recognition is not only social esteem.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is also the clarity of a pathway.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: People will invest in mastery when they see where the mastery leads.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, actively promote the message that skilled trades are essential work and a respected choice, not a back-up, not a second choice.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is about dignity and pride in the way that we work.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It matters for how young people, parents, employers perceive these pathways.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, we should ensure that the trade mastery translates into a good living.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want Singaporeans to stay in trades, real wages and progression must be clear and competitive.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, firms must be part of the solution.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I urge employers to support and fairly remunerate trade workers, and for the Government to work with the industry to build consistent standards for training, mentorship and assessment, especially in SMEs where the capability varies.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A strong local workforce will not be built on goodwill alone; it will be built on systems that make skills development, progression real.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, my question is this: as structured career pathways for skilled trades are being developed, I hope the Ministry can ensure that they are visible, trusted and outcome-driven, so that skilled workers can make real progression and real recognition, and young Singaporeans can see that trades are a first choice in a pathway to success.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, in Toa Payoh recently I spoke to a lift technician servicing one of our older blocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He shared that the systems today are far more complex than before.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: His job is no longer just mechanical repair, it requires interpreting system data, troubleshooting hybrid systems and ensuring safety standards are met.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is not low-skilled work but applied technical expertise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even the most advanced AI systems cannot repair lifts in our Housing and Development Board (HDB) blocks, maintain our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) trains and tracks or service precision manufacturing machinery all by itself.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we automate more processes, we need highly competent technicians who complement AI.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must invest adequately in skilled trades, so that we do not have high-end innovation without sufficient operational depth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From a wage and productivity perspective, if trade careers do not offer clear progression and competitive earnings, young Singaporeans would be discouraged from entering these sectors and local core would weaken over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there already signs of wage compression in middle-skilled technical roles and how might this affect the attractiveness of these careers to Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: True trade mastery takes years of apprenticeship, repetition and accumulated experience, which ought to be rewarded with a good and stable living.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Chairman, over the past decade, the Labour Movement has worked closely with tripartite partners to secure better wages, welfare and work prospects for our workers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our workers, including PMEs, have consistently seen real wage growth.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: PMEs now also have better support if they are retrenched through the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our young graduates have extra support to find work through the GRIT scheme.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Looking ahead however, technological and global economic shifts could result in more frequent employment disruptions for our workers, including and especially our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As our society enters a "super-aged" era, our workers will also face more intense caregiving demands.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: These changes will hit our workers, from the younger to the older, from blue collar to the white collar.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As such, we must do more to address their unique needs and challenges.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, I will focus my cuts to seek more support for our young graduates, PMEs and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: My fellow MPs have covered or will cover the other worker segments.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, let us do more to build up the career health of our young graduates from the onset.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many Members in this Chamber have spoken up likewise.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our young graduates are entering the workforce at a time when the nature of work is shifting.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In some instances, they need to outcompete AI at entry-level jobs, in others, they need to swiftly top up their skills with AI to be relevant.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Throughout their careers, they will likely need to adapt and pivot multiple times, as the pace of change and skills obsolescence increase.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I ask for MOM to be alongside our young graduates as they navigate these challenges.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must boldly rethink, refresh and re-shape our skills and jobs ecosystem so that workers, including the PMEs, can be better supported and enabled as they navigate the different stages of their careers, from graduation, all the way till retirement.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In making this move, we must endeavour to foster a better integration of business and workforce transformation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: From NTUC's experience, workers, including PMEs, are much more ready to upskill when they can see their training resulting in better wages or better work prospects.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In addition, when business transformation is done hand-in-hand with workforce upskilling, true value is unlocked because businesses can better incorporate AI into their business model, and workers can better apply what they have learned and share in the real productivity gains.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, can the Ministry share more details on how the merger between SSG and WSG will benefit our workers, including PMEs, in their career journeys from graduation to retirement?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, is the Ministry considering how to better integrate the various efforts across business and workforce transformation, together with Tripartite partners, as part of the new setup?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The second group I would like to speak for is our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: PMEs – especially mid-career, middle-income PMEs supporting their children and aged parents – are especially worried about the impact of retrenchments to them and their families.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In that light, I would like to ask the Ministry whether the Mandatory Retrenchment Notifications can be brought forward to enable earlier and better support to retrenched workers; and for the coverage of the current SkillsFuture JobSeeker Support Scheme to include our middle-income PMEs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The third group I would like to cover are our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As Singapore ages rapidly, more workers, especially the "sandwiched generation" in their 30s to 50s, will face dual pressures from caring for young children and elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Caregiving emerged as a key concern as early as 2023 in our #EveryWorkerMatters conversations.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: More must be done to support our caregivers to juggle work and caregiving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, let us move towards stronger institutional measures, including statutory paid caregiving leave, so our caregivers can stay employed, keep their skills current in a rapidly transforming economy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Second, provide caregivers who drop out of work due to caregiving with greater support and earlier assurance for their own retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The one-off means-tested Central Provident Fund (CPF) top-up to provide additional support to boost retirement adequacy of Singaporeans aged 50 and above is a step in the right direction, especially for our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: However, there is one group that I am particularly concerned about – the 13,000 or so who are out of the workforce to care for their elderly.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I note from MOM's data that this group is largely female, single, 50 and above, non-tertiary educated and do not have any or any recent work experience.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We think that there is scope to do more.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, as we become a super-aged society and live longer, having enough for retirement becomes critical.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I was glad to hear the Prime Minister's Budget 2026 announcement on the enhancements to the CPF Scheme to support our workers' retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We also look forward to the new voluntary CPF investment scheme offering life-cycle investment products.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: For many, the CPF Special Account was a familiar and stable way to grow their savings.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Following the closure of the CPF Special Account in 2025, some members expressed uncertainty about growing their monies to prepare for their golden years, especially after turning 55.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister share how this new scheme will be explained clearly to members, especially people who may not be familiar with investment risks and cannot afford to take such high risks?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: What guidance will be in place so they can make informed decisions, and not inadvertently take risks that they do not fully understand?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: I call on the Government to continue closely monitoring Singaporeans' retirement adequacy outcomes, more so for those who are needy, in vulnerable sectors, older and have lower CPF balances, given the transformation that is taking place.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Mr Chairman, the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) will be a game changer for the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: When I raised it in Parliament in January, I was glad to hear that MOM was in the final stages of implementation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: These few percentage points, over a long time horizon, could be the difference between retiring with anxiety and retiring with peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: This could also be part of the solution to address wealth inequality, given that the broad middle class has a significant amount of assets in CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: The CPF LRIS may not be for everyone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: As Mr Sanjeev said, individuals need to assess for themselves based on their own risk appetite.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Some may want their Ordinary Account savings to be more liquid for future housing needs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Others may prefer not to use their Special Account savings that earn 4% risk-free.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Overall, I believe the LRIS will benefit the majority of Singaporeans, especially if we can do the following.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: First, mount a large scale public education campaign over the benefits of taking long-term investment risk to achieve a higher expected return.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: This should not be routine public communications, but more of a sales pitch to Singaporeans on balancing long term, non-speculative investment risk for higher expected returns.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Second, make it as easy as possible to opt in for the LRIS, perhaps even make the LRIS the default option for some.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: For example, default Ordinary Account savings above the Full Retirement Sum into the LRIS, unless the CPF member opts out.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Third, add more friction for Singaporeans to speculate with the LRIS.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: For example, there could be cooling off periods.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: And those who want to sell before retirement could be required to attend a financial literacy course explaining the dangers of short-term speculation for non-professional investors.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh
text: Overall, with better financial literacy and wise behavioural nudges, we can empower more Singaporeans to optimise their lifetime of retirement savings and retire with peace of mind.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have been in the Chamber for the last five hours, so I propose to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to declare that I was a member of the CPF Advisory Panel.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, every Singaporean deserves a secure and adequate retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I support giving members more options, but I would like to emphasise three principles that should guide our design of the renewed system – complementarity, suitability and safeguards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The new scheme must be clearly positioned as an additional option and not a replacement for CPF's risk-free interest framework.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: For many Singaporeans, especially older workers and those prioritising certainty, CPF's guaranteed interest remains highly attractive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: CPFIS already exists for members who wish to actively invest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The new life-cycle scheme sits in between, for members who want some market exposure but prefer a professionally managed, automatically rebalancing portfolio.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our communications must allow all CPF members to appreciate the differences in the three options and to ensure that each option still serves the needs of a significant demographic of CPF members.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Even with this new life-cycle scheme, we should continue to refine the CPFIS.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Is this a result of the restricted products that can be invested in through CPFIS or some other reason?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: A 30-year-old with a long investment runway has very different risk capacity from a 58-year-old approaching retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: While the glidepath structure, reducing risk as members age, is sensible in theory, we must ensure members understand that: first, returns are not guaranteed; second, market downturns can occur close to retirement; and third, a shorter runway limits recovery time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Communications, especially to older members must be careful, balanced and transparent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Since CPF already offers a risk-free interest baseline, how will CPF Board ensure that the trade-offs of each option is sufficiently explained against their potential upside?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will there be clear scenario illustrations or simple decision-support tools, such as prompts based on age, years to retirement and risk tolerance, to guide members through the three alternatives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On product design, how will CPF Board calibrate the glidepath between growth and capital preservation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will there be more than one glidepath option to reflect different risk appetites?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The scheme also mentions phased liquidation before the target retirement date.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And how will liquidation be managed during periods of heightened market volatility?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will the scheme allow flexibility in selecting target retirement dates, as we extend working lives and members may retire later than 65?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: On fees, the objective is rightly to keep costs low and simple.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: How will providers be selected and what weight will be placed on long-term track record, risk management capability and operationalised resilience?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: And given the long lead time to 2028, has the Ministry considered piloting or phasing in elements of the life-cycle investment approach earlier, so that members can begin benefiting from it sooner?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, in my maiden speech less than a year ago, I noted that in this age of AI-driven disruption, conventional assumptions about career progressions and trajectories will fly out of the window.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The old patterns of career stability no longer apply.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: New graduates are having a harder time landing their first jobs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mid-career PMETs have to contend with greater career uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must all assume that there are no "safe" jobs anymore.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our workforce, up and down the value chain, must expect to not only upskill, but to reskill continuously throughout their working lives.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Lifelong learning is no longer just another buzzword, but a default in the new reality we are in.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must keep moving forward with our chin up and be ready to pivot and transition to new careers and industries, when necessary.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While some jobs and sectors are disappearing, entire new industries are also being born and many jobs are being redesigned and given new scopes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And employers are now struggling to find enough manpower with the skillset to match.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is the dichotomy that we are facing today.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: What we are seeing today is not just displacement, but a misalignment of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To empower our workers and businesses to navigate this fast-evolving jobs market, there is a critical need for us to refresh our career and employment services ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For that to happen, we need to take a holistic, big picture view of the whole ecosystem, and strike a new compact among all the stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is the baseline, the buck stops at the individual.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In this new reality, employers should not see their workforce in purely numerical terms, but as stakeholders in the longevity and well-being of their enterprise.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: An enterprise thrives only when its people thrive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Investing in employees is not a cost, but a long-term investment in resilience and growth.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Lastly, I see the Government as having the most central, overarching role.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must recognise that the career health of our workforce underpins the economic health of our nation.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government must ensure that the ecosystem we have in place is supportive of this effort.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It requires a helicopter view and a coordinated, forward-looking approach connecting education, training, employment facilitation and employer engagement.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our unions have a key supporting role in this.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The tripartite partnership has long been the cornerstone of our industrial relations and this collaboration will become even more important in a refreshed compact.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I think our unions as the ecosystem's transceiver, receiving and sending signals.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They act as a vital conduit between stakeholders, amplifying feedback and catalysing action.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, career health must first start in our schools.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our education system must keep pace with the rapidly evolving jobs landscape.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The young Singaporeans we prepare today must be ready for the careers of this brave new reality.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They must not only be skilled for the jobs of tomorrow but must also be equipped for the jobs of the day after tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This means having the right mindset, adaptability, resilience and capability of navigating uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Beyond the schools, we must ensure that the system also supports continuous upgrading and reskilling throughout working life.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government has done much in this regard.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are job-matching internship programmes for fresh graduates and mid-career workers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These are programmes to assist those who are keen to pivot to new careers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are support resources available for our workforce to reskill and upskill, and programmes to help who wish to, or who have to, transition into new roles.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There are also resources to cushion the fiscal impact while they do so.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Support exists for employers who are caught in the same choppy waters.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I personally see the tangible impact of these efforts.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am the Advisor to the Singapore Maritime Officers' Union (SMOU).

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I must note that most of these initiatives are by nature, reactive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government is the stakeholder best sourced to identify future trends, it can anticipate emerging disruptions and map out skills and capabilities that will be needed.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It can be seen that the broader patterns, the cross-sector shifts, the systemic risks and opportunities, and the Government can translate them into action.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It can help other stakeholders in the system stay ahead of the curve and bridge the disconnect between different stakeholders, bringing them together to match and realign resources, demand and skills.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, the buck may stop at the individual, but the Government has a critical role to play and I am keen to hear from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, as our economy shifts and AI reshapes how work is done, companies and workers are feeling the pressure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Younger workers want to know how to grow in an AI-enabled world and mature workers want assurance that they would not be left behind.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: HR professionals sit in the centre of helping both groups navigate this transition.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Singapore has made meaningful progress through efforts, such as the Industry Transformation plan, the Skills Framework for HR and the IHRP certification pathway.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These initiatives have raised standards and enabled workforce planning, job redesign and data-driven HR.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: These are real steps forward, but capabilities remain uneven, especially among SMEs with lean HR teams.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The HR sector needs practical and scalable support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: HR must shift from transactional delivery to strategic stewardship of human-AI work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I propose five priorities to further strengthen HR capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In fact, there are global companies that are developing such AI-solutions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Second, adopt skills-based workforce planning and scenario modelling.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Instead of focusing on headcount and budgets, we should support tools and advisory services that enable HR to model multiple future scenarios, anticipate role changes and plan redeployment and reskilling proactively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Third, reframe "job redesign" as job redesign for human with AI.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: This is not incremental tweaking of jobs given automation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We must use design thinking to integrate AI with human judgement, empathy and creativity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The Ministry can fund playbooks and pilots to test new role models and measure outcomes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Fourth, scale people analytics and predictive decision support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: HR needs data literacy, analytics tools and predictive models for turnaround and internal mobility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Subsidies for analytic tools and targeted training will help HR teams make evidence-based redeployment and retention decisions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Fifth, make HR a key steward of AI ethics, transparency and trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: HR can take the lead in ensuring these safeguards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Chairman, with rapid change and in a talent-scare economy, companies struggle to attract, develop and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Strengthening HR capabilities is essential to help companies thrive and support Singaporeans through their multi-stage careers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: A merit-based workplace must give workers confidence that they have a future in a transforming economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: PWM has made important strides in raising wages for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: PWCS has supported both workers and employers through this adjustment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We thank the Ministry for extending PWCS for another two years and note that PWCS, in its present form, was meant to be transitional.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
