text: But in an era of AI disruption and given our structural limits on workforce expansion, productivity growth must increasingly come from upgrading jobs, not simply adding manpower.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This makes our lower-wage workers more exposed to displacement risks if transformation outpaces reskilling.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: An important policy intent behind the PWCS, introduced in 2022, was to serve as transitional support to help businesses defray their costs of raising the incomes of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Critically and for the purposes of my cut, the scheme was not conceived merely as wage support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: MOM expected employers to use the transitional period to upskill their employees, transform their businesses and improve productivity so that wage increases for workers will be sustainable over the longer term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It cannot be the case that there is no report back to Parliament on the outcomes these subsidies have achieved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A policy review could also reveal the important gaps to assist future policy-making with regard to manpower levies and quotas and whether they should be adjusted, for instance, identifying sectors where upscaling of business transformation has reached a practical limit given current technology.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Conservancy cleaning in the HDB setting is a case in point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Productivity improvements in this sector are marginal, and robotics has not advanced to a point where machines can sweep common corridors across different floors and independently negotiate staircases at a commercially viable price point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: With assistance through the PWCS scheme running into the billions of dollars, Parliament must be expected to track the policy impact of this initiative and to determine whether further extensions are warranted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if so, whether expected business outcomes should be imposed to ensure that taxpayers' subsidies deliver for both businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the alternative, if the intention is simply to support businesses without strings attached, so as to force wages up at the lower end, then that should be communicated as such rather than to seek outcomes which for some employers may simply not be realistic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Adult caregivers are the invisible backbone of our society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They care for ageing parents, chronically ill spouses, children with rare conditions and family members in need.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They do this quietly, faithfully, often at great personal cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My Woodlands resident, Mdm A, spends about 12 hours a day caring for her elderly parents and aunt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She has not had a full night's sleep in months.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She told me she feels isolated, guilty and trapped and yet, she continues, because the family depends on her.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It sometimes forces caregivers to leave the workforce altogether.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And yet, when their responsibilities ease, returning to work is not simple, especially after years away.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When parents are stretched thin, children may receive less attention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Those in lower-income households may receive fewer enrichment opportunities and reduced exposure to pathways that expand social mobility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today's caregiving responsibilities can quietly shape tomorrow's inequalities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I welcome enhancements to the Caregivers Training Grant and the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But much more can be done to better understand and alleviate the inter-generational impact.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe we must go further in three areas: relief, retention and re-entry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can we expand practical respite and navigation support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we reduce the social isolation they face?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we ensure their children do not miss out?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can we strengthen incentives for FWAs and provide structured coaching at key transition points, so caregivers do not have to choose between career and care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can we create structured return pathways so that stepping up for family does not mean stepping back professionally.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Today, I want to reframe it as a workforce challenge, one unfolding quietly in our workplaces right now.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Many colleagues are part of the sandwiched generation, managing ageing parents while holding full-time jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: These exits do not show up as unemployment but represent a massive loss of experienced talent.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's ageing population means eldercare responsibilities will only grow.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We have made tremendous progress supporting working parents.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It is time we extend similar support to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Workers age 40 to 59, our most experienced professionals, are stepping back not by choice but because they lack structured workplace support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We are losing productivity and institutional knowledge when we can least afford it.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Current measures help caregivers after they have left the workforce through reskilling programmes and re-entry support.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We need proactive workplace support that prevents exits.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Those with multiple care recipients would receive two additional leaves.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The recent Tripartite Guidelines on FWA requests are a start, but we need employer frameworks that make eldercare support standard practice, not discretionary.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We must normalise eldercare conversations, just as we have normalised childcare discussions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Start with data collection to understand the scale, pilot workplace frameworks with willing employers, develop realistic best practises across sectors.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Research shows employees who balance work with caregiving face higher stress and reduced productivity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Supporting them through structured leave can improve well-being while paying it for itself through better retention and productivity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: By the time someone needs reskilling to re-enter the workforce, we have already lost years of their contribution.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: Supporting eldercare is not just a compassionate policy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: We cannot afford to lose 87,000 workers, many in their most productive years, to a challenge we have simply chosen not to address proactively.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: The question is not whether we can afford to act.

speaker: Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik (Sengkang)
text: It is whether we can afford not to.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Mr Chairman, our senior employees aged 50 and up bring deep domain knowledge and hard-earned experience.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: It enabled more workers to attain the Basic Retirement Sum from six in 10 in 2016, to seven in 10 in 2022, and I am glad that CPF has projected eight in 10 will attain this by 2027.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: However, senior workers find themselves increasingly juggling caregiving and wishing for more work options, so they can strike a better balance between work and life.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on what is being done to enable more work options and expand the availability of FWAs?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: At the same time, many senior workers and jobseekers who are 10 to 15 years away from the statutory retirement age worry about ageism and displacement amid rapid technological changes in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Many senior workers and jobseekers have told us that there are fewer opportunities for career advancement and good jobs later in their career.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Younger cohorts are also convinced that this is the case.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Others have shared that while they are willing to upskill and learn, their long work hours, caregiving duties after work, unfamiliar learning formats and the uncertainty of translating these to better work prospects are also practical barriers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Can the Ministry share how it plans to intervene at mid-career stage to boost continued employability for workers before they reach their late-50s?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: I therefore welcome the announcement of the extension of the Senior Employment Credit scheme to 2027, to continue supporting hiring or/and retaining of senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: This sends an important signal to firms that senior workers remain valued contributors and provides some cost relief that is especially important for SMEs amid the hyper-competitive business environment.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari
text: Will the Ministry considering extending this Senior Employment Credit beyond the end of the 2027 review?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: They are important, but they do not address a key concern of younger Singaporeans, like myself, which I had raised in Budget debate last week, that we will not have the time or energy to be present parents.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: For many of us, the structure of working life in Singapore makes parenthood feel like a compromise, not a choice.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Last week, Minister Indranee called for a society-wide reset on how we view and support marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I hope the Government will lead by example with the reset, beginning with a new lever – time, specifically to move from intention to impact on flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: The enforcement mechanism, when that process is not followed, is for an employee to approach the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I believe it means that they are not being used.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: One complaint is not a sign of success.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: It is a sign of a barrier too high to clear.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: While legislation alone cannot change workplace culture, it can set a floor.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: It can signal that the Government is serious about the mindset reset to support Singaporeans in building and growing their families.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: As a starting point, I have two suggestions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: An employer who fails to engage properly or who rejects a request without genuine business grounds, should face consequences.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I welcome the extension of the Senior Employment Credit and the CPF Transition Offset, but they are not enough.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Training grants exist, but too often they feel one-size-fits-all.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: One 72-year-old man told me: “They keep pushing me to AI courses, but that is too far a stretch for me.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It will not help me actually get a job.” Other seniors face physically demanding roles or inflexible workspaces.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Offices, factories and retail spaces are often designed for the young and able bodied.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Many do odd jobs, which provide neither security nor opportunity to contribute their expertise and experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: So, I ask the Minister, can we give seniors tailored training that actually fits their capabilities and abilities, and dedicated support to place them in jobs that actually fit their lives?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can we help seniors better navigate SkillsFuture course options so they can actually use their credits?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can we redesign workplaces, especially for SMEs in sectors like retail, logistics and services to be more senior friendly?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Lighter duties, flexible hours, assistive tools, mentor-type positions, so experience is valued as much as energy?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Can we give grants and tax incentives for businesses that make all this possible?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: These interventions complement, not replace, existing wage support schemes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If we want seniors to remain independent, we must redesign work, not just subsidise it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I also note the extension of the part-time re-employment grant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Could MOM share the uptake and outcomes so far?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And could we expand practical models so seniors can pace themselves while staying engaged?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And with the Tripartite Workgroup on senior employment, when can we expect key recommendations and how will success, beyond placements, be tracked?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Let us ensure our seniors do not just live longer, they thrive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Let us ensure they do not just earn a living, they contribute, mentor and lead.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Let us ensure they do not just survive, they succeed.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Diana Pang, kindly deliver your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This clarity reduces misunderstanding, builds confidence and encourages constructive and mature workplace dialogue.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These guidelines promote work-life balance and provide a clear, structured pathway to request flexibility in where they work, when they work, or the workload they take on.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This is especially important for parents, caregivers and those managing health conditions, enabling them to remain economically active while meeting family and personal responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For employers, the guidelines introduce discipline and transparency.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Employers are expected to respond in writing, and where requests are rejected, to explain clearly based on business needs.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This reduces speculation, limits perceptions of bias, and strengthens trust and workplace harmony.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: While TAFEP provides grants, templates, training and advisory services, real operational challenges remain.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: On the ground, SMEs face five key pain points.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, manpower constraints, with small teams lacking dedicated HR capacity.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, management constrain on supervisors as they have to handle both hybrid and staggered work schedules of their team.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, performance and fairness concerns, including tracking output, fears of misuse and perceptions of inequality.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Fourth, higher operational costs, such as information technology investments and extra manpower for shift cover.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Fifth, operational and contractual constraints, especially in sectors such as F&B, retail, security, where physical presence is essential.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, if we want a fair and inclusive workplace, they must also be sustainable for the employers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For without employers, there are no employees, vice versa.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As we strengthen worker protections, we must equally strengthen support for SMEs to implement these guidelines in a practical, proportionate and business-viable way.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I will now speak on the importance of building a safe, inclusive and fair workplace for the employment of people with disabilities, women and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, we must strengthen protection against workplace discrimination and harassment, including bullying that is often subtle and not immediately visible.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: All employers want a safe and respectful workplace, but many SMEs struggle with policy design, complaint handling, documentation, deciding on appropriate responses, especially without in-house HR expertise.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It can take the form of verbal intimidation, gaslighting, passive aggression, repeated put-downs, hostile tone, public shaming, deliberate exclusion, or constantly shifting expectations.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These behaviours may leave little paper trail on the outcast, but over time they erode trust, undermine psychological safety and drive attrition, which is a lose-lose outcome for both employees and employers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Protections must therefore be real, accessible and consistently applied, but we should not assume that employers are always the wrongdoers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Sometimes, the misconduct comes from fellow employees as well.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This system should help employers intervene early, guide them on proper complaint handling and provide workers with a safe, trusted channel to report concerns.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, inclusive employment for persons with disabilities, women, and caregivers is both a social good and make economical sense, especially in a tight labour market.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Strong support frameworks can help these groups fulfil their care-giving aspirations and maximise their contributions.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But for inclusion to work, we must look beyond the employee barriers and also consider employers' capacity to implement it.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For SMEs, inclusive hiring can bring sudden operational costs, job redesign, additional supervision, workflow adjustments, training, managing healthcare and well-being concerns.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we want inclusive hiring to be sustainable, employers must be supported, not overwhelmed.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Fairness means wider opportunity, reduced biasness and progression based on performance and potential, but fairness must also be sustainable.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Inclusive policies, flexible arrangements and stronger protections will succeed only if they are credible to workers and workable for the employers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Many SME bosses operate under immense pressure, paying off staff before paying themselves, managing cashflow risks, meeting compliance requirements and carrying all the emotional burden of keeping their businesses alive.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Ultimately, a fair workplace cannot exist without the well-being of both the employers and the workers.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But even so, one death is one too many.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This reminds us that employer mental well-being also matters.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: With this in mind, I offer four suggestions to the Minister.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Chairman, I hope the Minister will consider the issues I have raised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: This reflects the sustained efforts of workers, employers and the Government.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: But every life lost at work is one too many.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: We must now take the next decisive steps.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: First, workplace safety and health (WSH) must evolve to reflect our ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: As retirement and re-employment ages rise, longer careers must also be safer careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Risks such as falls, musculoskeletal disorders and fatigue cut across all industries, not just traditionally high-risk sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: They should redesign jobs, automate hazardous tasks and eliminate risks at the source.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Safer work design must become the norm, not the exception.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Where safety technology has been proven to reduce accidents, adoption should not remain voluntary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: If these technologies save lives, we should require their use.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Government can also do more to drive change.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Second, fatigue must be treated as a core safety issue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Guidelines are a good start, but guidelines alone are insufficient.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: While I welcome the enhanced dormitory standards, dormitories should be better integrated with surrounding communities, with accessible healthcare, recreation and essential amenities closer to where the workers live.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: They are commitments to dignity, responsibility and fairness.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: If we know what works, we must mandate it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: If we see what harms, we must redesign it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: And if we set standards, we must enforce them, because every worker deserves a safe and healthy workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: While workplace issues have been closely examined, we must not forget the living conditions of our hardworking migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Many spend most of their time between dormitories and worksites, with limited opportunities to relax, socialise, or build community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Prolonged separation from families can also affect emotional well-being and heighten isolation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I acknowledge the Ministry's efforts to improve our dormitory standards.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Beyond this, I call on the Ministry to continue investing in measures that strengthen our migrant workers' access to amenities and community spaces, ensuring that our migrant workers' living environment supports well-being, dignity and of course, social integration.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to take this opportunity to wish everyone a very Happy Chinese Valentine's Day.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Geopolitical conflicts, as seen from recent developments over the weekend, are upending the world as we know it and reshaping global trade and investment flows.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: AI is transforming how we work and our workforce, too, is evolving.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This year, Singapore will become a super-aged society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we seek new growth frontiers, we must ensure that our growth remains inclusive and that it creates meaningful careers for all.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We start from a relatively good position today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Despite a challenging global environment, Singapore's labour market remains resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The labour market remained tight in 2025, with more vacancies than jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was bolstered by productivity improvements and targeted wage support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These outcomes reflect our workers and businesses' resilience and contributions, and investments in growth areas, like AI and advanced manufacturing, as well as very good collaboration with our tripartite partners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will continue to walk with workers and businesses, so that every worker, every worker matters and every worker can realise their potential, achieve their career aspirations and every business can thrive by bringing out the best in their people.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together with our tripartite partners, we will: one, empower Singaporeans to build meaningful careers; two, enable businesses to transform and provide quality jobs; and three, build more inclusive workplaces that leave no one behind.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To our youths, we are committed to giving you a strong start to your careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Transforming from school to work can be daunting, especially with the angst and anxiety over how AI is changing entry-level jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Fortunately for us, the market for fresh graduates remains resilient, at least for now.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over four in 10 openings are entry-level PMET roles suitable for young graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By December 2025, over eight in 10 university graduates from the 2025 cohort had already found employment and this is comparable to the 2024 cohort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to prioritise creating more full-time opportunities for fresh graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While vacancies are available, some graduates do indeed face challenges in finding the right match.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To support them, we introduced the GRIT scheme last year, alongside GRIT@Gov for the public sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: GRIT helps our graduates acquire structured, industry-relevant work experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers have told us that GRIT has helped them increase hiring amidst a more cautious environment and they intend to emplace good performers onto full-time positions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We incentivise employers to do so by continuing subsidies for trainees emplaced during the traineeship period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Take Ms Jewel Goh and Mr Dominic Wong, two recent graduates who started their traineeships at DBS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Jewel, who has a diploma in Applied AI and Analytics, was given the opportunity to apply what she has learnt to support DBS' technology systems and large-scale operations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Dominic, a Communications graduate, got the chance to develop partnerships with DBS' stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am sure that their GRIT experience has given both graduates more clarity and confidence to take their next steps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: GRIT remains open to graduates from the 2025 cohort and we will extend applications to the 2026 cohort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If market conditions call for it, we may expand capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Several Members have made suggestions on supporting our youths.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Gerald Giam suggested introducing wage support for SMEs to hire graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim proposed a national apprenticeship programme to strengthen on-the-job training.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These suggestions are in line with the Government's ongoing efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been enhancing work-based learning and on-job training through schemes, like the AI Apprenticeship Programme and the SkillsFuture Work-Study Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Work-Study Programme has grown significantly and as the Ministry of Education shared earlier on, the Work-Study Diploma programme will be enhanced in line with the Economic Strategy Review's (ESR's) recommendation to support flexible pathways that blend training and working throughout life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are also subsidising 70% of traineeship costs through GRIT.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we will continue to study such suggestions and look into more ways to support our fresh graduates, we should also design our support carefully and sustainably.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, GRIT sources the traineeships from leading companies in growth areas, ensuring that our graduates gain high quality experiences and stronger long-term prospects.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A broad-based wage subsidy for SMEs to hire graduates may not provide the same quality of experience, if companies lack the capacity to train them or provide meaningful careers once the subsidies end.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A general subsidy may also entail even more wastage, given that 80% of our graduates have been able to secure jobs within months after graduation without such wage subsidies today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Additionally, we also have to balance against unintended outcomes, where companies might end up retrenching older workers and replace them with cheaper graduates so that they can save on manpower costs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, our approach on balance is appropriate for the present situation, where many full-time roles remain available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To help match graduates to such roles, we have stepped up career guidance and employment facilitation efforts through WSG, e2i and the IHLs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond this, overseas work stints help and equip Singaporeans with the necessary skills and perspectives for a globalised economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Providing early opportunities strengthens our talent pipeline and our companies' global competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond a strong start, we will also ensure that all workers have the resources to thrive throughout their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will do so in four ways: by building an AI-ready workforce; helping workers navigate the labour market with confidence; developing our local professional talent pipeline; and supporting displaced workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One of our foremost priorities is to build an AI-ready workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A recent report by McKinsey, EDB and Tech in Asia found that about three in five Southeast Asian firms have yet to see meaningful financial gains from AI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is partly due to a lack of internal expertise and low employee adoption.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We cannot afford to let this gap persist.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To translate the potential of AI into good jobs for Singaporeans, we will take decisive steps to build an AI-ready workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Like learning a language, developing true fluency in AI comes from consistent use and building confidence through experimentation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, we will make it easier for Singaporeans to have hands-on experience and access to the latest AI tools.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM has been engaging providers, such as Google, Manus, Microsoft and OpenAI.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will announce details in due course, including the tools and platforms that qualify.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Assoc Prof Terence Ho suggested for AI access to be extended even more widely, including to mature and lower-income workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I agree that access should be inclusive, regardless of age or income.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, this initiative will be open to all Singaporeans aged 25 and above, and they are paired with practical and accessible training for AI at various levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond this, we will continue to explore ways to include more mature and lower-income workers in our national AI journey.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While an AI-ready workforce offers significant potential to improve productivity, we must steer AI adoption to enhance our workers' potential, not displace, not replace it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will elaborate later on our support for employers to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will help workers better navigate the labour market and seize new opportunities with confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To this end, we are fundamentally reviewing our jobs and skills ecosystem, which Ms Gho Sze Kee spoke about earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have four goals, the "4Vs": volume, we want to reach a larger share of the workforce; variety, we want to cater to more diverse needs in a complex job market; velocity, or speed, matching people to opportunities more quickly; and value, value-add, supporting long-term career health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Its mission will be to empower Singaporeans to develop future-ready skills and access good job opportunities; enable businesses to create good jobs for Singaporeans and develop their workforce; and promote a culture of lifelong learning and career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng asked how this merger will benefit Singaporean workers, and how we will better translate training into employment and productivity gains.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Eileen Chong said that the new agency should not just support workers, but also employers, to take forward SSG's ongoing efforts in encouraging skills-first hiring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, our skills and employment facilitation capabilities sit in separate agencies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Bringing them together under one roof creates a single, powerful engine for human capital development.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It will collaborate with other agencies and stakeholders to benefit both workers and employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For workers, this means simpler access and more integrated career support in a fast-changing marketplace.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It means a single portal to access training, career guidance and job opportunities, without having to navigate multiple agencies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By combining career and skills data, we can give you a clearer picture of where opportunities are, enabling better-informed career and training decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the employers, the merger will help us be even more responsive to your talent needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With more timely and comprehensive labour market and skills insights, WSSG can help to reduce skills mismatches and time-to-hire.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Creating a single point of contact will also simplify how we support businesses to address hiring, training and workforce transformation needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: WSSG will play a critical role in expanding the career health movement, going beyond reactive job matching, to proactive career planning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As outlined in the handout distributed to Members, we have initiatives targeting both workers and employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For workers, we launched Career Health SG last year with a fundamental message – stay proactive, pre-emptive about your career.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nearly two-thirds of our workers now see value in improving their career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many are still unsure as to how to begin.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, starting on your career health journey does not have to be that overwhelming.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have been building practical tools to help our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Careers and Skills Passport lets you take stock of your skills, and CareersFinder helps you to discover the job options that you may not have even considered.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those who need even more personalised support, we have expanded access to career planning programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Almost nine in 10 respondents reported having clear direction and greater confidence after attending such programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Following the integration of Careers and Skills Passport with job portals, JobStreet and FastJobs, our partners found that job applications with verified credentials are 1.5 times more likely to be shortlisted by employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are expanding our Careers and Skills Passport partnerships to five more job portals – MyCareersFuture, Careers@Gov, EASE, FindSGJobs and eFinancialCareers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also integrated Careers and Skills Passport with HR tech firm JobTech's platform, enabling employers to search for candidates based on verified skills data.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For employers, tools, like TalentTrack and TalentTrack+, can help you better assess your workforce readiness and identify internal talent for new roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through WSSG, we will also strengthen our ecosystem of career and employment service providers to serve different workforce segments more effectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As our workforce evolves, new forms of career support are needed – some of which can be delivered effectively through private service providers specialising in certain industries, certain sectors or workforce segments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, WSG has partnered Ingeus and AKG, two private job matching firms, to provide more specialised support for PMEs since 2017.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have observed higher re-entry rates among those assisted, compared to retrenched residents in general.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To take this further, we convened the Alliance for Action on Advancing Career and Employment Services (AfA-ACES).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, for the individuals, for fresh graduates, we will test services combining career guidance and industry exposure to support your school-to-work transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For mid-level professionals, we will pilot personalised career agents to help you move into better roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For caregivers, seniors and those facing greater hardship, we will explore new ways to support you to work more flexibly, or better still, get you to return to work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For SMEs, we will test ways to support your own internal mobility and also perhaps, suggest to you, adopt new work models.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These efforts will also help address concerns about underemployment, which Mr Patrick Tay had requested updates on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM has been studying underemployment in the form of overqualification, where workers possess higher educational qualifications than typically required for the job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Preliminarily, we found that most overqualified workers in Singapore took up their current jobs voluntarily, for reasons such as flexibility or planned career transitions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The share of involuntarily overqualified workers remains small and stable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our efforts to strengthen the career and employment ecosystem will better support these workers to find jobs more aligned with their aspirations or develop the skills to enter such jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will release detailed findings later in the year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, for Singaporeans who aspire to leadership positions, we will help you develop the skills to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the past year, we have expanded the capacity, the uptake of our professional development programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the support from EDB, the Singapore Leaders Network run by the Human Capital Leadership Institute has grown to over 4,000 members, with new and expanded offerings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes the Overseas Transition Support programme, which has supported already about 120 professionals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at the same time, I want to reassure you, new opportunities will arise, and we will help you to seize them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last year, we launched the SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme, which provides temporary financial relief and job search support to involuntarily unemployed individuals, helping them regain their footing and return to work with confidence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The scheme has made a difference for many Singaporeans, but we can do more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just as what Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng and Mr Patrick Tay have suggested, expanding the scheme’s coverage beyond the current qualifying income cap.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Jobseeker Support scheme has been in place for about less than a year, we are reviewing the scheme and its parameters when we have more experience.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we will ask for your indulgence and patience in supporting us through this journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will provide further updates on the scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Singaporeans lead longer and healthier lives, we must shift from managing the pressures of ageing, to unlocking the benefits of career longevity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will give our seniors more flexibility and assurance, while enabling employers to retain experienced workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond how long we work, we must also transform how effectively we work by creating more flexible and varied pathways for seniors to remain engaged and productive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment is studying a more integrated approach to support career longevity, including enabling individuals to plan earlier for later-stage career transitions, and equipping employers to design age-friendly jobs and workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share more about these initiatives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we will continue to strengthen our retirement adequacy policies to give our seniors greater assurance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have been enhancing the CPF system over the last few years, providing Singaporeans with more support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This has only been possible because of our strong social compact and belief in shared responsibility between individuals, families, employers and the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will better support retirement adequacy for seniors who wish and want to take the option to continue working.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With this, we have reached the target contribution rates for senior workers aged above 60 to 65, as recommended by the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will extend the CPF Transition Offset for another year to help cushion half of the increase in employer CPF contributions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Later this year, we will also announce the new retirement sums for cohorts beyond 2027, to allow members to better plan ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With rising living standards, the new retirement sums will better reflect the savings needed to meet basic retirement needs in the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For seniors who may face challenges in building up enough savings despite their best efforts, we are committed to support you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The top-up will be automatically credited this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, the CPF system offers risk-free interest of up to 6%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members seeking potentially higher returns can invest through the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS), which has around 700 products available.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, this requires financial knowledge and active investment management.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This helps to calibrate exposure to investment risk at different life stages and it mitigates market downturn risk when it is time to exit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To keep choices simple, we will curate to two to three reputable commercial providers offering a small number of options.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree with Mr Saktiandi Supaat that for many Singaporeans, especially older workers and those prioritising certainty, the CPF risk-free returns remain highly attractive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Not everyone has the appetite for investment risk.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members who prefer to actively manage their own investments can continue to invest their Ordinary and Special Account balances via the CPFIS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members can also opt to retain their savings in their CPF accounts to continue earning risk-free returns.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree with Mr Shawn Loh, with Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari and Mr Saktiandi Supaat that investor literacy is key.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members must understand the products and their risks, and decide the most suitable option for themselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will work with the selected product providers and partners, including the Monetary Authority of Singapore to enhance investor education.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I also want to thank our Members for their suggestions on product design, such as on cooling-off windows, the target date and encouraging retention.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More details will be announced in due course.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling requested an update on how we will refresh our foreign workforce policies to generate growth and good jobs for Singaporeans, while recognising the limits to which we can keep growing our foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thriving businesses are the engine of good jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Before joining the Government, I was in the private sector all my life, so I can understand the angst faced by private entrepreneurs and business owners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thriving business, they are engines of good jobs, rising wages and they continue to sustain opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In a fast-changing global environment and under tighter resource constraints, businesses can only thrive by continuously transforming their business models and investing in their workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, enabling business transformation remains central to our foreign workforce strategy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to remain globally connected and open to talent that can complement our skilled local workforce, while reducing reliance on foreign labour where there is scope to raise productivity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will make further enhancements to our foreign workforce policies in line with this approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we will continue to compete globally for top-tier talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since the launch of the Overseas Networks and Expertise (ONE) Pass for pinnacle talent in 2023, there has been healthy growth in take-up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He is an Assistant Director at the A*STAR Genome Institute of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He developed Fragle, which is a novel AI-based method to monitor cancer progression and relapse through blood tests.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Or Mr Oliver Jay, Managing Director at OpenAI, whose experience in bridging Silicon Valley and Asia supports Singapore’s ambitions as a leading AI hub.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Previously, Mr Jay spent two years mentoring Singaporean leaders in high-growth Singapore companies such as Carousell and Glints.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will replace the Tech.Pass and offering more attractive terms than the Tech.Pass.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, we must stay open to skills and expertise from abroad while ensuring they continue to complement our local workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our EP and S Pass Qualifying Salaries are regularly updated to keep pace, they are keeping pace with local wage benchmarks – they do not lead the local wage benchmarks – so that it ensures that foreigners who come here do not compete mainly based on accepting lower salaries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will apply to new EP applications from 1 January 2027 and the renewals from 1 January 2028, to give employers time to adjust.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond meeting the qualifying salary, EP applicants must also pass COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay requested an update on how our COMPASS framework incentivises firms to improve their workforce profile.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since implementation about two-and-a-half years ago, in 2023, about two-thirds of the current EP holders have passed through COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Results suggest that we are moving in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The share of firms with higher dependence on foreigners of a single nationality has decreased by 20%, while the share of firms with a higher dependence on foreigners in general has decreased by 37%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the S Pass, we will continue to raise the minimum qualifying salary in line with wages of the top one-third of our local associate professionals and technicians (APTs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the first step, we will raise the minimum qualifying salary from $3,300 to $3,600.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will apply to new applications and renewals from 1 January 2027 and 2028 respectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By around 2030, if the economy continues to grow, the S Pass minimum qualifying salary is expected to be around $4,000 to $4,500.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, like I said, the caveat is it depends on our prevailing local wages and the prevailing economic conditions then.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With an ageing local workforce, Singapore needs Work Permit Holders to deliver essential infrastructure, goods and services.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we agree with Ms Yeo Wan Ling that our Work Permit growth must be sustainable, given our infrastructural and social constraints.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our businesses must operate more efficiently by adopting technology and redesigning jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we have grants to help companies to do that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, even as we manage numbers, we will continue to support businesses in accessing higher quality, the key thing is higher quality, Work Permit holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To this end, we will make two enhancements to our Work Permit framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we will streamline our Work Permit levy framework to make it easier for businesses to understand, and they can plan how they hire, how they can train and how they can retain the Work Permit holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, for the Marine Shipyard and Process sectors, we will work towards aligning the levy rates with Construction.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is set to incentivise companies to hire higher-skilled workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, our exhortation is for companies to bring in higher-skilled workers, retain them and train them well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the Manufacturing and Services sectors, we will combine the bottom two tiers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For this new combined tier, the levy rates for the Higher- and Basic-skilled workers will be $300 and $470 respectively for Manufacturing; and $400 and $600 respectively for Services.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The higher-skilled workers will enjoy a lower levy compared to the relatively unskilled workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we will retain existing levy rates for the highest tier, so that firms with a higher reliance on Work Permit holders will continue to pay higher rates because we hope that they can work with us to redesign, to improve and transform their work processes to achieve higher productivity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This revised levy schedule will take effect from 2028.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are giving a heads-up in advance so that companies can plan for it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will work closely with industries to strengthen the framework for identifying higher-skilled workers eligible for lower levies in each sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The NTS-OL allows businesses to hire higher-quality non-PMET workers from non-traditional source countries for specific roles with not enough locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Mark Lee shared the challenges of domestic-oriented sectors that operate on thin margins and rely on S Pass holders for frontline roles, such as F&B.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the upcoming expansion of the NTS-OL to include four more F&B roles, including frontline waiters, businesses can retain these workers who may not meet the higher S Pass qualifying salary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Both Mr Mark Lee and Mr Shawn Loh raised an important point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We need to be pro-worker and we need to be pro-business.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They have asked how MOM considers sector needs and business costs when calibrating our policies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our policy changes are developed in close consultation with sector agencies and with industry partners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where essential or strategic areas have limited scope for automation or localisation, MOM works with sector agencies to provide targeted foreign manpower flexibilities, calibrated to avoid entrenching labour-intensive business models.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We closely monitor business cost increases, keeping in mind Singapore's continued ability to attract investments and talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Between 2019 and 2025, profit rates in Singapore grew by 4.4% per year, indicating that businesses have been improving profitability alongside cost increases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore was also ranked the most talent-competitive economy in the 2025 Global Talent Competitiveness Index.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, we are ramping up business cost support measures through targeted wage credit schemes, which Senior Minister of State Koh and Minister of State Dinesh will elaborate on further later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We understand that businesses need time to shift towards more productive models and, therefore, we announced, ahead of time, we implement changes at a measured pace and phased out approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To succeed, firms must invest in developing their workers to take on new and redesigned jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As announced last year, the Government has set aside over $400 million for the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Working with the Singapore Business Federation and SNEF, the scheme aims to strengthen the link between enterprise transformation and workforce development, capturing growth and creating jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked about the implementation of the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package, the SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+) will be rolled out in March 2026, this month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This builds on the earlier Support for Job Redesign under the Productivity Solutions Grant programme (PSG-JR), which supported smaller-scale projects, leading to improved retention and wage growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+) will expand support significantly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Enterprises can now receive up to 70% of project costs capped at $150,000 per company, which is higher than the PSG-JR cap of $30,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will allow companies to redesign more roles, engage experts to build internal capabilities and implement AI-native workforce solutions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Assoc Prof Terence Ho has asked how Singapore can build expertise in human-centric job redesign, ensuring that AI augments rather than replaces human contribution.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do so through initiatives, such as the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package, which couples productivity support with workforce support.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also worked very closely with NTUC through the Company Training Committee programme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through WDG(JR+), enterprises can work with consultants to assess their AI readiness, identify opportunities and redesign roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can also receive support to implement workforce technology solutions, such as AI-powered HR tools.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to improve access to AI support under Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package, with pre-packaged solutions targeted at specific company needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To further drive workforce transformation efforts, we must also develop our HR leaders and professionals because these are the people behind the people.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To uplift human capital management standards, we formed a Tripartite Workgroup on Human Capital Capability Development last year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Workgroup has made important progress in developing strategies to strengthen firms' HR capabilities, such as through establishing clear benchmarks for human capital performance and expanding professional HR practice to more organisations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh will share more on the Workgroup's recommendations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Economic growth and business transformation must go hand-in-hand with fairness and inclusion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our workplaces must continue to provide every worker with safety, opportunity and dignity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the past, success in the labour market was narrowly defined by academic qualifications, linear career paths and traditional professions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Increasingly, there is greater awareness that there are diverse pathways to success, and every profession deserves recognition and respect.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the Prime Minister said, inclusive growth also means creating good jobs in domestic and essential services where many workers are employed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Economic Strategic Review has also recommended broadening the range of good jobs in our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Assoc Prof Terence Ho has identified several areas where we can redesign jobs to attract more young Singaporeans, including healthcare and skilled trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Prime Minister has outlined how we are increasing pay and progression in the education, healthcare and social service sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are working with the Labour Movement and trade associations to make similar efforts for the skilled trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree with Ms Diana Pang and Mr Saktiandi Supaat that the skilled trades can and should offer good job opportunities for those who prefer "hands-on" work that require dedication and mastery.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many such trades will remain essential in our future economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They may also be resilient, or even complementary, to automation by AI.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Electrical work, for example, will remain indispensable in our transition to a green and AI-powered economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Yet, with the workforce ageing in such trades, we need to think harder about workforce renewal and attracting more Singaporeans to join these trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are young Singaporeans that are building fulfilling careers in the skilled trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, Mr Koh Jia Xing, an electrical engineer with Syntigro Engineering Ptd Ltd.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having trained in aerospace engineering at ITE, Jia Xing decided that he wanted to embark on a career in electrical engineering.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In his career thus far, one project stood out for him – replacing a hospital's main electrical switchboard, with the hospital still fully operational.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Believe you me, I have run hospitals before and any outage will result in a significant compromise in human lives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, this is high-stake, very challenging work, but it is one that gives a sense of fulfilment, and that pride in how skilled tradespeople can keep critical systems running.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, Jia Xing is pursuing a Masters in Electrical and Electronic Engineering at the Singapore Institute of Technology.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have started with the electrical trade given its essential role in our future economy, that it has deep skills content and the need to build a strong local pipeline.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will learn from this to scale up our efforts to other trades.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will provide updates at a later stage.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have received feedback from businesses that MOM's policies add to costs, and many employers are feeling the squeeze amidst tight margins.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not just hear you, I empathise with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But at the same time, I want to also share with you a different perspective, that our manpower policies also serve important social objectives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As highlighted in the Ministry of Finance's Occasional Paper on inequality, policies such as our PWM play a crucial role in achieving inclusive growth and prevent social fissures from deepening.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The majority of labour-related business cost increases arising from Government policies go towards uplifting wages for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Without such policies, our lower-wage workers will fall further behind, just as Singapore's Gini coefficient showed before the introduction of the PWM in 2012.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government will nevertheless continue to help our businesses to mitigate the cost pressures that you are experiencing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Shawn Loh and Mr Liang Eng Hwa suggested extending or making PWCS co-funding permanent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Meanwhile, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Pritam Singh asked how PWCS can be better tied to productivity outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our policies strike a balance between these two perspectives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Productivity improvement is key to achieving sustainable wage gains.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The PWM is central to these efforts, linking wage growth to skills development, career progression and job redesign.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, productivity improvement can be uneven across sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In domestically oriented sectors where many of our lower-wage workers are employed, it takes time to redesign labour-intensive work processes and it also takes time to allow our lower-wage workers to upskill into new roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, on top of broad-based enterprise transformation measures, we introduced the PWCS, temporarily cushioning the near-term cost impact of moves to support lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This ensures that support remains a catalyst, not a substitute for productivity improvement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The PWCS is reviewed regularly to provide adequate support to businesses while they transform.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just as crucially, as Ms Yeo Wan Ling highlighted, this ensures a manageable pace of change for lower-wage workers to upskill into new roles, limiting disemployment risks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many companies have made good use of Government support to innovate and evolve alongside their workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Likewise, over 600 companies have taken up the PSG-JR since 2020.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That said, we must continually renew our efforts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In response to Mr Melvin Yong, we have some ways still to go to boost productivity growth in PWM-covered sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As highlighted by the Singapore Productivity Centre’s Food Services Productivity report, improving productivity is essential for resilience and sustainable growth, especially for firms in sectors facing manpower shortages, competitive pressures and rising operational costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is fully committed to walking alongside employers and lower-wage workers on this journey.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I spoke earlier about some of the initiatives we will be rolling out to this end, including the Enterprise Workforce Transformation Package.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These efforts are aligned with the Economic Strategy Review's recommendation to broaden the range of good jobs across our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Dinesh will share about how we will further support upskilling for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ultimately, uplifting our lower-wage workers is a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We hope employers will take advantage of support to deepen their transformative efforts and lower-wage workers will seize the upskilling opportunities to move into higher-value jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members, including NTUC Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng, spoke about the challenges faced by caregivers, including the "sandwiched generation".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to encourage inclusive workplace practices, supporting workers who may face higher barriers to workforce participation such as women, caregivers and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Shawn Huang will provide updates on these efforts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As work evolves, our employment framework must remain fit-for-purpose.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The tripartite partners are reviewing how the Employment Act can continue to provide appropriate safeguards for different worker groups, including updating coverage and protections for our most vulnerable workers under Part 4 of the Employment Act.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also looking at how to provide businesses with greater flexibility and efficiency in workplace management, and to streamline key provisions for easier compliance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We aim to ensure that our employment framework remains trusted and relevant, upholding a harmonious and equitable labour compact where both workers and businesses can thrive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested mandating advance notification prior to retrenchment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Ng Chee Meng also asked whether Mandatory Retrenchment Notifications can be brought forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While advance notification has merits, mandating such a requirement poses non-trivial challenges.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Retrenchment is often, in fact I would say, is always a difficult process for all parties involved and is often a last resort for companies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And many a time, senior management, together with the board, conduct backroom negotiations to try to save as many jobs as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we mandate advance notifications, this may inevitably or inadvertently push companies to finalise retrenchments faster, discouraging such negotiations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Pritam Singh suggested that Singapore legislate retrenchment benefit, with larger companies paying a higher amount.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have said before when we pushed for the Workplace Fairness Act that legislation is not a panacea.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We protect our workers but at the same time we need to give businesses some flexibility to adjust in different situations because retrenchments occur for a whole variety of reasons.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And company size is also not an indicator of a company's ability to afford retrenchment benefit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So it balance, we are reviewing it, and I think Senior Minister of State Koh will provide further updates on the Employment Act review.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Every worker deserves to return home safe and healthy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workplace safety and health (WSH) is a shared responsibility that involves all of us – employers, workers and Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Dinesh will update on moves to strengthen and improve WSH ownership.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Dinesh will also update on our continuing efforts to ensure our migrant workers' well-being.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, I will now speak in Mandarin, please.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In Mandarin):   Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the way we work and, this year, Singapore will also become a super-aged society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some Singaporeans may feel anxious about the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the economy transforms, the Government will ensure that our nation's growth remains inclusive and that it creates good, meaningful jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of the important steps we are taking is to harness the potential of AI to create long-term, quality employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not a competitor, and it is definitely not the exclusive domain of young people.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will ensure that Singaporeans have the support they need at every stage of their career.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also help graduates from Institutes of Higher Learning establish a solid foundation for their careers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the ancient saying goes, “Even in the twilight years, a hero's ambition does not fade.” With age comes experience, not retreat.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The experience and wisdom of our senior workers are the strongest assets in our workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Please be assured that regardless of the stage of career you are currently in, we will walk alongside with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will help you to continuously keep pace with the rapidly changing job market and stride towards the future with confidence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the poet Li Bai has written, “There will come a time to ride the wind and break the waves, let us set our sails straight and cross the vast sea.” As long as we remain confident and move forward hand in hand, we will surely forge ahead despite the difficulties and create a better tomorrow. : So, to conclude, Mr Chairman, the road ahead will be neither certain nor easy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we have proven over the last 60 years that we can overcome any challenge as long as we are prepared to tackle them collectively together – we did it before and we will do it again.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our strong labour market and wage outcomes, they are the result of deliberate choices for us as a society, as a country and as a people to invest in our workers' skills and development, support business transformation, uphold fairness and trust in our workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we will continue to ride and build on this momentum.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have all got to play our part.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workers will have to take ownership of their career health, businesses will have to continue to transform, and the Government will continue to walk alongside all of you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Tripartism will remain the corner stone of our strength.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And it is through trust and partnership, through our tripartite way, that we have weathered past challenges.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will collectively shape a future of work where every one of us can contribute with confidence, grow with purpose and we can look ahead with confidence and assurance, come what may.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, our workforce has always been the backbone of Singapore's progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Singaporeans live longer and healthier lives, we now have the chance to extend that progress into longer, more rewarding careers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the past, a career often progresses in a linear fashion, with people starting in one job after graduation and working their way up through the same company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But today, faster business and technology cycles and changing business models mean that most people will go through multiple jobs and roles over their working lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Workers now have different work-life balance expectations and different hierarchy of needs at different stages of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For workers, this means that careers are no longer about climbing a corporate ladder, but rather about navigating a dynamic, multi-stage journey – moving up, across domains or even intentionally downshifting to balance life's priorities, such as caregiving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This also means taking greater ownership of their careers and skills and desiring more flexibility in work arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For employers, this shift means more than just adapting job roles, it means rethinking how jobs are designed to tap on both the vitality of youth and the wisdom that comes with seniority and experience, how talent is managed and developed at every stage and how transitions are supported across a workforce that is increasingly diverse in age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
