speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: With this expansion, around 24,000 Singaporeans with disabilities below the age of 55 can benefit from the scheme this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: But inclusive workplaces cannot be built on incentives alone.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: That is why MOM is working with tripartite partners and social service agencies on a new Tripartite Advisory on Reasonable Accommodations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: The Advisory will provide practical guidance on how reasonable accommodation can be implemented at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: This gives employers clarity, and for workers, confidence to raise accommodation needs early.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Nevertheless, workplace demands are evolving, and many families wonder if their loved ones with disabilities can adapt.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: That is why last December, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the formation of the Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities, chaired by Minister of State for Social and Family Development Goh Pei Ming, and supported by myself and colleagues from the Ministries of Education and Health.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, “The sea embraces all rivers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: It is great because it is inclusive.” In this rapidly changing era, the Government's goal is very clear.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We want to help every employee continuously improve and move towards success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We firmly believe that an inclusive workplace environment will benefit all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Employees can better utilise their strengths and companies can also recruit more outstanding talent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: MOM will continue to spare no effort in strengthening Singapore's labour market.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Although we have already achieved some results in promoting workplace inclusivity, we understand that some Singaporeans still face challenges when seeking employment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Moving forward, MOM will further improve systems to create more employment opportunities for them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: Allowing women and employees who need to care for their families to better balance career and family responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: These measures are not only practical but also complement each other to create a conducive work environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong)
text: We want to create inclusive workplaces that allow workers to achieve their career aspirations and participate meaningfully in the workforce.

text: Employers must build a culture where every —

text: Guillotine time is 7.00 pm, so we only have about 25 minutes before we have to end this Head.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: One is with regard to Minister Tan's speech earlier about GRIT and OMIP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can Minister share a bit more about that?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The second one is I am happy to hear just now about the Overseas Markets Immersion Programme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is very important as Singapore tries to internationalise.

text: Second question is with regard to my question on the skilled trades.

text: I hear Minister mentioned just now about the sectoral move to create the electronic or electrical trade framework.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Why not do that national rather than a specific sectoral, because I think we may be too slow if we do on a sectoral basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I do not know, maybe can hear from Minister his view on that, given that the medium- to long-term manpower projections for critical skilled trades might be in need.

text: The last question I have is in terms of the life-cycle investment scheme.

text: I asked a question in my cut, whether the scheme will allow for flexibility in selecting target retirement dates as we extend working lives and members may retire later than age 65.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have as of the outset about 4,000-plus applications, but I do not have the exact numbers with me, but the vast majority of them actually found jobs while they were applying for GRIT, because they contemporaneously also apply for jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we are happy for that, because the whole objective of GRIT was to place them into permanent jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are still quite a substantive number out there that are undergoing on board clearance, including some security checks as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we are heartened to see is that by the end of January and into February, like I said, the majority of the original GRIT applicants have actually found jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to hold it and, depending on the requirements, we may expand it if necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the Overseas Markets Immersion Programme, we are also very heartened by the response.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we are now doing is to expand it to more companies, to even potentially to younger employees as well who join companies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The most important thing that we require the companies who participate in the the Overseas Markets Immersion Programme, the funding is actually quite generous, it is up to 70%, it is for them to have a clear business plan.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There must also be a very clear career path.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What are the roles that they are going to transition post that overseas attachment?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With that, with our programme partner and WSG dispersing the grant itself, we hope to be able to reach out to a larger swathe of the young population.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the last one, the CPF Investment Scheme, and then maybe the Member could tell me what was the second one.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The investment scheme is meant to provide a longer-term horizon for younger CPF members at the point of either starting or maybe very early on in their careers when they have a runway.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we have taken, with getting consultation with many of the investments consultants and advisors is that, we wanted to set it such that that life-cycle product allows for first, an automatic rebalancing without the member having to actively manage the portfolio with age; and the second part is obviously once they reach a certain age, then there would be a liquidation, a phased liquidation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As far as what is that time horizon and whether we can extend it, today, we are just about to talk to the different providers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When we get more information, and once the scheme runs over the course, not the entire course at this time, once we have got the experience in working with some of these providers, we would be able to continue to refine and tweak the scheme further.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having said that, even at our Payout Eligibility Age of 65 today, we find that quite a number of our CPF members have opted to get the payout at 70.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And in fact, many of the members have asked us, can we extend beyond 70?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, ostensibly we understand, we take all this feedback into consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are all living longer, hopefully healthier and these are the considerations that we will constantly take back and review.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We wanted to start with three sectors, because obviously there are multiple sectors all over.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the first one we work with was the electrical trade.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Part of the reason is that I am very familiar with the electrical trade, because I happen to also cover energy in the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our licensed electrical workers (LEWs), they are also rapidly ageing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, if I am not mistaken, the median age of our LEWs is about 60, 60 something.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I think for our own resilience, for our own security and our own reliability, we have to train this group of people.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And earlier on I mentioned Jia Xing, I think he has done very well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we want to start that on a very firm footing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The other two trades that we have identified is plumber and then the third one is air-conditioning technicians.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I think the Member knows the size of our population.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we want to try to spread it too thin, then obviously how to differentiate according to the importance and so on, I think that impact would be a lot more less impactful compared to being very focused on these three.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are starting off with these three first.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Chair, if I heard Minister Tan correctly, he indicated the Government generally subscribes to the principles of on-the-job training through a traineeship programme, such as GRIT.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if so, does he anticipate that there will be a clear timeline for this expansion?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A big part of it, of course, is the expectations may not match the type of jobs that are available in the market today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we are considering for GRIT is for a group of graduates who may need the additional internships.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Suffice to say, today, we already have a whole series of all these programmes available – GRIT, Overseas Markets Immersion Programme, and these are for junior level persons.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond that, even at the mid-career level, we have also got different types of attachment programmes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When it comes to the finance sectors and so on, I believe that WSSG would have to work with the Monetary Authority of Singapore, with the Institute of Banking and Finance Singapore and maybe other specialised institutions to get traction and to make sure that our reach and our impact is optimised and maximised for our locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think we all want the same thing for our people.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to ensure that we deliver the best outcomes for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Would MOM consider expanding a Company Training Committee-style support, specifically for mid-career PMEs, who face possible disruptions and to enable employers also to redesign the roles and redeploy staff more proactively, because the Company Training Committee support could act like a enterprise-wide thing to allow for the health diagnostics, career health diagnostics, then the co-funding of the renewal and then the multi-stage career planning.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, I would like to ask if that would be possible?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The other is in terms of planning ahead and integrating a multi-stage career, would MOM explore sector-specific adaptations of the multi-stage career pathways particularly for sectors that are facing disruptions, for example, structural shifts, manufacturing, professional services and ICT?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And finally, on caregivers, there has been a lot of discussion about giving caregiver support for employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But for those who have already been disrupted and are trying to enter the workforce, what additional support could be given to them, to help them re-enter the workforce?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The answer is yes, because the Company Training Committee structure and the format is really a means to an end.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, if there are companies today, even before we start with the Career Longevity Centre, for example – even today, any company that is keen to do a more systematic transformation of their workplace in the business model, together with bringing workers along, can already approach NTUC, where there is a team of dedicated industry training officers that can guide a company through a Ops-Tech road mapping process and then chart out the road map for them to do a Company Training Committee-style transformation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That can affect the whole entire company's workforce, not just for the mid-careerists.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second question on whether there will be sector-specific multi-stage pathways.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is one area of thinking we are looking at as well, because as I said in my speech, there is no one-size-fits-all model that will work for all companies or for all sectors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in order to have a little bit more of a targeted, tailored-made kind of a pathway for companies, we think that the AfA concept of what we are doing by having companies from different sectors piloting some of the ways in which they help to transform into a multi-generational workplace.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They could then start to share their learnings with fellow companies in the same sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is one approach that we can take.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How we can actually then enlarge this could be through the various trade associations and chambers or even through the Career Longevity Centre, where employers themselves can conduct conversations and workshops, share their own experience, so that SMEs and companies of different sizes can learn together, have a community of practice and that then takes away some of the fears of even embarking on this transformation of the workplace, by the companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that concept is exactly what we are thinking of.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How we operationalise it, is something that is still in discussion and we are open to ideas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The third one on how we can help caregivers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If we can get our career and employment support ecosystem, as Minister and myself had articulated, up to speed, crowding in a lot more of the private sector players in this space as well, some of the resources that we put forth, not just for the senior workers, can also be useful to those caregivers who have left the workforce for some time, who needed maybe a bit more of a skills uplift.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the concept of the Career Longevity Centre or the combination of WSG and SSG coming together can do, is indeed in that direction, to put a one-stop kind of service for those who may need not just upskilling, but also have a bit more planning on how they can re-enter the workforce, and eventually find a better way to manage their entry into the workforce, perhaps even consider a case management-type of approach.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In other words, the caregiver who may have been out of the workforce for some time, you cannot just leave the person alone to just, "Oh, here is a job, and good luck to you.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is between you and your employer." Maybe a case management approach to check in on the person, to just find out how you are doing after the first few months, to just make sure you handhold not just the individual, but maybe work with the HR in the company to understand how the HR for the company can better support this person who may need a lot more guidance, being away from the workforce for some time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, these are ideas we are all exploring right now.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, for your five cuts, totalling seven minutes.

text: How does it differ from the current Tech.Pass, and who are we really hoping to attract?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We believe that the three most valuable traits that we have collectively is our one people, the trust that we have built over the years and the credibility that we have as a hub.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And of course, today, in the uncertain world that we live in, the safety, the predictability, the transparency and the frameworks that we have here, and the type of robust debates, the constructive debates that we were able to have here, in the House, all put us in a very good position to attract global talent to be here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And with that, they can spawn multiple enterprises.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can uplift the calibre of all, by transferring cutting-edge technology, thought processes and so on to our locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Then I think we would have arrived and achieved our end objective.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, you had four cuts, totaling 10 minutes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In the Labour Movement, I have seen first-hand how PWM brings dignity, structured progressions into our workers lives when previously there was none.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In this House today, I heard differing views questioning the relevance and efficacy of our PWCS and, thereby, impacting the PWM productivity and upskilling intents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: When something has demonstrably improved livelihoods for thousands of Singaporeans is portrayed as burdensome or ineffective, it risks eroding confidence in policies that have made actual differences on the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: There has been a diversity of views expressed today, including specific suggestions to policies, how will the Government take all of these on board?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I recognise and I respect the diversity of the views that have been expressed, not just today, but I think in many of our sessions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And there are also many different views, huge dichotomy and also many tensions between the views that have been expressed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, some would want AI to move faster and then others urge more caution.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have even had Mr Gerald Giam and Assoc Prof Ho, who called for rapid AI democratisation, put AI skills into every workers' hands, as quickly as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Then, we have got other examples where some want to raise productivity skills and wages in the domestic sectors, while others ask to support lower productivity sectors with easier access to foreign workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, Mr Chairman, these are examples that reflect the fundamental trade-offs that we must all square off.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the Government of the day, we are entrusted with the responsibility to navigate these complex issues.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have to reconcile all of these tensions into coherent, fiscally sustainable and forward-looking and practical policies for all of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We consult widely with workers, with employers, with unions, with industry partners and we try as much as possible, to ensure that the voices and the concerns are heard.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to empower Singaporeans through all stages of life and we want to ensure that they are equipped to succeed in this changed world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also have to contemporaneously ensure that our businesses continue to thrive in this transformed landscape, so that we can continue to foster an environment where innovation, where opportunity continues to be accessible to all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sometimes, certain, very expedient and clear pathways may seem so intuitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Why is it that we are not able to do it?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is because whatever policy that we come up with and implement, it will trigger a cascade of ramifying effects, much further, laterally and down the line.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And hence, we walk on a very tight rope and we hope that with your support, with that focus on singularly building a better future for all of our Singaporeans and our future generations that will come after us, we will continue to work hard to build a Singapore that is prosperous, that is full of optimism, resilient and safe for all.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I thank the Member for her understanding.

text: So, can I invite Ms Yeo Wan Ling, if you would like to withdraw the amendment?
